title: The Lost Colony of Roanoke: What Does CROATOAN Really Mean?
description:
At daybreak on August 18, 1590, an English ship lowered a small boat off Roanoke Island. Before landing, the men sounded a trumpet and sang, and no one on the island answered. Three capital letters were carved on a tree, and on a post stripped of its bark at the palisade entrance, five feet above the ground, a whole word was carved. There was no cross above the word, and the governor who had come back for his people wrote that seeing it actually made him glad.

This episode goes through the file in the order things happened and came to light: why they stayed on Roanoke three years earlier, the joint statement the colonists signed, the sign agreed on before he left and the cross that was never added, why supplies could not reach the island in the year of the Armada, the days when only one of four anchors was left, the 1709 retelling, how the name "the Lost Colony" grew up in the 19th century, the worst drought in 800 years, read from tree rings, the ring that tested as brass, and the opposing claims of two excavation teams today.

Every popular version is marked as a later addition; where sources disagree, we say they disagree, and where nothing is settled, we say so. The source of every number, year and quotation is listed in the references below.

The illustrations in this episode are AI-generated. Historical figures are drawn as cartoon characters, unnamed and not made to look like anyone; living or recent people are not drawn, and appear only as generic figures in plain clothes, seen from behind or from a distance.

Information as of 2026-10-10

ro201.text: He was glad because the word was his own agreed sign.

ro202.text: This man was John White, governor of these colonists.

ro203.text: On July 22, 1587, they reached the Outer Banks.

ro204.text: They aimed north, for Chesapeake Bay.

ro205.text: There they'd build houses and a fort.

ro209.text: Sources give anywhere from about 100 to 150.

ro210.text: The old fort was razed, melons grew in empty houses, and deer fed inside.

ro211.text: On August 18, his granddaughter was born there.

ro212.text: Remember the date he landed? August 18.

ro213.text: The day he stepped onto the empty island was her third birthday.

ro214.text: Yet four days later, all the colonists came to him.

ro215.text: They asked him to sail home for supplies himself.

ro217.text: On August 25, they signed a joint statement.

ro218.text: Two mornings later, he set sail.

ro219.text: His granddaughter was just nine days old.

ro220.text: Before he left, they agreed on a sign.

ro221.text: If they moved, carve the place name.

ro222.text: If in danger, add a cross above the word.

ro223.text: Above the word on the post, there was no cross.

ro224.text: By their agreement, no cross meant they were safe.

ro225.text: He thought he'd be back soon.

ro301.text: But in those years, England was at war.

ro303.text: The Queen ordered all English ships held at home.

ro304.text: That April's supply ships fought the French and turned back.

ro305.text: The supplies never reached the island.

ro306.text: Back ashore, he wanted to go south.

ro307.text: The name carved was an island down the Outer Banks.

ro308.text: That island is around today's Hatteras Island.

ro309.text: It was home to the Croatoan people.

ro311.text: But that first August, the English had attacked them by mistake.

ro313.text: Of four anchors, only one was left.

ro314.text: He wrote that the weather grew worse daily.

ro315.text: Water casks still lay on shore, not aboard.

ro316.text: They chose: south for water and winter, back next year.

ro317.text: On August 28, a storm drove the ship toward the Azores.

ro318.text: Then they went home to England.

ro319.text: No one ever reached that island.

ro320.text: No record says the English saw them after that parting.

ro321.text: But one thing in White's own account doesn't add up.

ro322.text: He wrote they were preparing to move 50 miles inland.

ro323.text: Note that number; it will return.

ro324.text: But what the post said didn't point inland.

ro401.text: The southern islanders later told a story.

ro402.text: In 1709, the traveler from the start wrote it down.

ro403.text: Hatteras people told him some of their ancestors were white.

ro404.text: And that they could talk to a book, as the English did.

ro405.text: It's a retelling from long after, and the only one.

ro406.text: Another claim is darker: a great chief inland ordered them killed.

ro407.text: The man who wrote this heard it secondhand.

ro408.text: And what we remember today is a different line.

ro409.text: That day, White also saw three capital letters carved on a tree.

ro410.text: But over time, it became a word carved on a tree.

ro411.text: Who first said so can't be traced.

ro412.text: Stranger still, even this case's name came later.

ro413.text: In the 1830s, a book and a magazine article described it this way.

ro414.text: An 1837 novel seems the first to use that name.

ro417.text: That year, the first carved stone appeared.

ro419.text: Most were later judged to be fakes.

ro420.text: Is the first one real? No one can say.

ro421.text: But that island's soil held something else.

ro501.text: In 1998, a university dug into a patch of sand on that island.

ro502.text: They found a ring, then said to be gold.

ro503.text: That same year, elsewhere, someone was counting tree rings.

ro504.text: That study read rainfall from the rings.

ro505.text: It said 1587 to 1589 were especially dry.

ro507.text: But it measured regional trees, not the Outer Banks itself.

ro508.text: The paper itself only says drought may be linked to this.

ro509.text: But here's the catch: drought can't explain that word.

ro510.text: The ring is what sent people back to dig there.

ro511.text: In 2009, locals formed an archaeology group.

ro512.text: Later, a British university joined in.

ro524.text: The other team, though, began with a map.

ro601.text: In 2012, someone spread out White's map at the British Museum.

ro602.text: On that map was the patch from the start.

ro603.text: Under the patch was a fort-shaped symbol.

ro605.text: The symbol under the patch is at that distance.

ro607.text: Two sites dug there yielded objects Europeans used.

ro513.text: In spring 2015, Hatteras Island gave up part of an iron sword hilt.

ro516.text: In 2017, the ring from the start was sent for testing.

ro517.text: It turned out to be all brass.

ro518.text: Things found with it date from 1670 to 1720.

ro520.text: Most European items there were mixed in with mid-17th-century material.

ro521.text: Peers say they're hard to date precisely.

ro522.text: They may have come later, by trade.

ro608.text: In 2020, the inland team's own archaeologist said something.

ro609.text: One of the sites wasn't the main place they moved to.

ro610.text: That same year, a university archaeologist said he was skeptical.

ro514.text: In early 2025, Hatteras Island yielded buckets of hammer scale.

ro515.text: So far, only the diggers say so, in interviews.

ro523.text: The southern trail is still unsettled today.

ro611.text: Then, in June 2026, the inland team's foundation changed its tune.

ro612.text: On its own website, it announced the Lost Colony was found.

ro613.text: That announcement had no new dig report.

ro614.text: We've seen no third-party review yet.

ro615.text: Nothing from those two sites can be confirmed as theirs.

ro616.text: So can anything at all be confirmed as theirs?

ro702.text: The US National Park Service updated its page in 2025.

ro703.text: No remains, no graves, no houses can be definitively tied to them.

ro704.text: Joining the Croatoans is just one of the most popular theories.

ro705.text: Two scholars who wrote a whole book say their answer is: we don't know.

ro706.text: My view: the hard part isn't the word, but what came after it.
